claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr has a single-phase BCC structure in the stated initial condition.
The initial alloy contains grain boundaries and subtle compositional variations that act as microstructural heterogeneities.
Thermal-expansion mismatch at microstructural heterogeneities generates localized internal residual stresses.
These mismatch-generated residual stresses are a common governing cause of creep, temperature-dependent elastic moduli, cold-rolling strain hardening, and aging-induced hardening.
Introducing a minor secondary phase with a different expansion coefficient can engineer a thermal-expansion mismatch in HfNbTaTiZr.
Applying a controlled thermal gradient during solidification can engineer a thermal-expansion mismatch.
Homogenization can minimize thermal-expansion mismatches and yield a near-uniform internal-stress state.
Mismatch-generated residual stresses interfere with dislocation motion.
Mismatch-generated residual stresses affect phase stability.
Mismatch-generated residual stresses modify high-temperature creep rates.
Mismatch-generated residual stresses alter work hardening in cold-deformed samples.
During aging, mismatch-generated residual stresses affect phase evolution and strengthening.
Secondary precipitates at grain boundaries can affect alloy plasticity.
The magnitude and distribution of mismatch-generated residual stresses become more pronounced as differential thermal expansion increases.
Engineered-mismatch samples will have creep rates different from those of the baseline at approximately 1250 °C.
Engineered-mismatch samples will exhibit anomalous nonlinear temperature dependence of elastic moduli between 293 and 1100 K.
Engineered-mismatch samples will exhibit modified hardening during cold rolling and aging.
The proposed effects are strongest above approximately 600 °C because thermal-expansion differences are largest there.
More severe cold rolling can produce greater directional differences in thermal-expansion behavior than a 20% reduction.
